title: Steamed Syrup Sponge
subtitle: A classic British steamed pudding with a golden syrup base
excerpt: Golden syrup poured into a pudding basin, topped with a butter sponge, and steamed for two hours until the sponge is fluffy and the syrup has caramelised to a glossy, sticky sauce. Turn it out at the table.

recipe.sourceNotes: Steamed puddings are a British culinary tradition with roots in medieval boiled puddings, which used cloth as the mould. The ceramic pudding basin with a paper-and-foil covering replaced the cloth by the Victorian era. Syrup sponge — a simple creamed sponge with golden syrup in the base — became a domestic standard partly because Lyle's Golden Syrup was introduced in 1881 and quickly became one of the most recognisable products in the British kitchen. The pudding has appeared in Delia Smith's Complete Cookery Course and countless cookbooks since as an exemplar of British comfort food. The golden syrup forms a sauce around the sponge as it steams: when turned out, it cascades down the sides of the pudding.

recipeTools.notes: A saucepan large enough to hold the pudding basin on a trivet.

content.text: Butter the basin very thoroughly, including the rim, so the pudding turns out cleanly. The pleated paper cover is important: the sponge expands as it steams and needs room to rise. Keep the water at a steady simmer for the full two hours and top up with boiling water as needed. Test doneness with a skewer through the paper.

content.text: Butter a 1.2-litre pudding basin generously. Spoon the golden syrup into the base. Beat the butter and sugar until pale and fluffy. Beat in the eggs one at a time. Fold in the flour, vanilla, and milk until just combined.
Spoon the sponge mixture over the syrup. Level the top. Cover with a double layer of greaseproof paper and a layer of foil, pleated across the middle to allow for rising. Secure tightly with string.

Place the basin on a trivet in a large saucepan. Pour in enough boiling water to come halfway up the sides of the basin. Cover and steam over steady medium-low heat for 2 hours, checking and topping up with boiling water every 30 minutes. The sponge is ready when a skewer inserted through the paper comes out clean.

Remove from the pan and leave to rest for 5 minutes. Run a knife around the edge of the basin, place a deep plate over the top, and invert firmly. The pudding will drop out with the syrup running down the sides. Serve with custard or cream.
